# mdÂ²

mdÂ² is an open-source Kanban-style tracker for software development that is built around plain markdown files instead of a database, and treats AI coding agents as first-class citizens of the workflow â€” not an afterthought bolted onto a card.

Every piece of work â€” a feature, a bug, a job â€” is a single markdown file with a small structured header (id, status, owner, affected files, ...) and a body written in normal prose. Nothing is hidden in a proprietary format: the "database" is just a folder of `.md` files in a git repository, so it can be read, diffed, grepped, and edited with any tool you already use, and it works equally well as a home for human notes or as context an agent can read and write directly.

## Why cards, why markdown

- **The board is the repo.** Cards live in a working folder inside your project's GitHub repository (or, when paired with the desktop app, a local git checkout). A card's `status` field determines which column it appears in â€” move a card between columns and its file is updated (and committed) accordingly.
- **No lock-in.** Because everything is markdown with a light front-matter header, a project's history is legible without mdÂ² at all. Renaming, templating, and searching all just operate on files.
- **Agents read and write the same files you do.** A card's body is the brief an agent works from, and an agent's output â€” logs, generated diffs, follow-up questions â€” is linked back to that same card, so a human and an agent are always looking at the same source of truth.

## How it works

- **Two views on the same data:** a **card view** (kanban columns driven by card `status`, drag-and-drop reordering, inline title editing, policy indicators) and a **text view** (a folder tree next to a tabbed markdown editor), so you can work at the level of the whole board or dive into a single file.
- **Actions** are the operations you can run against a card â€” anything from "implement this feature" (dispatched to an AI agent as a configurable prompt) to a lint/test script or an arbitrary shell command. Actions can chain (`before`/`after` steps), branch on their own output via regex conditions, and fire automatically on state changes (e.g. dragging a card into "in progress" kicks off an "implement" action).
- **Agent-aware by design.** When run inside its companion Electron desktop app, mdÂ² can launch coding-agent CLIs directly, stream their stdin/stdout/stderr into logs attached to the card, and let you continue an existing agent conversation with a single click â€” from the card, or from a split view in the editor.
- **Data layer with two backends.** In the browser, mdÂ² talks to GitHub's API directly (sign in with GitHub, work against any repo/branch). Paired with the desktop app, it additionally gets direct local git and filesystem access, so agent actions and file edits can happen without a network round-trip.
- **Everything else is configurable:** card types and ID schemes, markdown style presets, the color theme (light/dark, round-cornered, borderless "flat" look), and the set of available actions are all driven by project configuration rather than hardcoded.

mdÂ² is still an evolving concept â€” see [design/architecture/initial description](design/architecture/initial%20description) for the original design notes this project is built from.

## Getting started

1. Install the app.
2. Click the GitHub icon, upper left corner, follow link to get a GitHub access token, copy-paste token in.
3. Open project, select a folder that contains a git repository.

## Development setup

The repo has three parts: [app/](app/) (the React/Vite web UI), [desktop/](desktop/) (the Electron host shell), and [shared/](shared/) (types and logic used by both). Each subproject has its own `package.json` and npm scripts, but a root `package.json` wires up the common workflows.

### Prerequisites

- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (LTS) and npm
- Git

### Install

```powershell
npm run install:all
```

This installs dependencies for both `app` and `desktop`.

### Run

```powershell
npm run dev
```

This starts the Vite dev server for `app` and, once it's up, launches the Electron shell (`desktop`) pointed at it. To run either half on its own: `npm run dev:app` or `npm run dev:desktop`.

### Optional environment variables

`app/.env.example` and `desktop/.env.example` list optional Sentry/Aptabase keys for error reporting and analytics. Copy to `.env` and fill in if you want telemetry locally â€” neither is required to build or run the app.

### Lint & test

Each subproject is standalone and has its own npm scripts.

```powershell
cd app
npm run lint
npm run lint-fix
npm run test
```

```powershell
cd desktop
npm run lint
npm run lint-fix
npm run test
```

messages.content:
Your task is to prepare this project for development.

Instructions:

1. Start by locating and reading the \`README.md\` file in the current directory.
2. Follow the setup instructions in that README exactly.
3. If the main README refers to additional \`README.md\` files in subdirectories, or if subdirectories contain setup instructions that are required for development, read those as well.
4. Perform all necessary project setup steps, including (where applicable):
   1. Installing dependencies.
   2. Installing toolchains or SDKs.
   3. Restoring packages.
   4. Creating generated files.
   5. Running bootstrap or setup scripts.
   6. Initializing git submodules.
   7. Installing workspace/package manager dependencies.
   8. Building any required generated artifacts.
5. Do not start long-running processes such as development servers or watch tasks unless the README explicitly requires them as part of setup.
6. If any step requires user input, elevated privileges, secrets, credentials, or external configuration, stop and explain exactly what is needed before proceeding.
7. If multiple package managers or setup methods are available, use the one recommended by the project's documentation.
8. If the documentation contains conflicting instructions, prefer the instructions in the top-level \`README.md\` and explain any conflict.
9. When setup is complete, provide a concise summary including:
   1. The steps that were performed.
   2. Any issues or warnings encountered.
   3. Any manual steps the developer still needs to complete.
   4. Whether the project appears ready for development.

Do not make assumptions beyond what is documented. Base your actions on the project's documentation whenever possible.

I’ll inspect the repository’s setup instructions, package manifests, and current dependency state, then perform only the setup steps the project explicitly defines and verify the development checks that are available.

The repository defines three dependency sets: root tooling plus `app` and `desktop`. The documented `install:all` installs only the two subprojects, so I’m also checking the root tooling explicitly; telemetry `.env` files are optional and I will not create empty local copies.

Node.js 22.16.0 is installed, but VS Code’s auto-attach debugger is injected into terminal Node processes and caused the first npm probe to stall. I’ll clear that injection only for setup commands, then install the locked dependencies in each project.

All three dependency sets installed successfully. I’m now validating the prepared workspace with each subproject’s required lint and test commands; dependency deprecation notices came only from transitive Electron-side packages.

Lint and test validation is still running across both subprojects. No failures have been returned yet; the app test suite is the longer-running part.

The combined validation wrapper hit its timeout while the app’s Vitest process was still running, so it did not preserve the completed check outputs. I’m rerunning the checks independently with an appropriate test timeout so the final result is unambiguous.

Both linters pass cleanly. The desktop test runner is active but has not emitted per-file progress; I’m allowing the project’s full suite time to complete rather than treating the earlier wrapper timeout as a test failure.

The app suite passes all 1,223 tests. Desktop completed 447/451, with four failures concentrated in Git/filesystem tests: three hit the fixed 5-second timeout and one timing-sensitive worktree assertion then left a locked temp directory. I’m rerunning only those files with one worker to distinguish environmental contention from a real setup problem.

The isolated desktop rerun is still executing, which confirms this machine’s Git-backed tests are unusually slow relative to their 5-second per-test limits. I’m waiting for the final pass/fail output before deciding whether any project change is warranted.

The four previously failing desktop files pass when serialized. I’m now running the entire desktop suite with the same one-worker setting so the final development baseline reflects a complete passing suite, not just targeted reruns.
